quote: the time at which it asserts the one to be different and the other to be different is not accidental to the assertion
claim: The temporal moment of discriminating differences is essential, not accidental, to the act of discrimination

quote: it asserts thus—both now and that the objects are different now; the objects therefore must be present at one and the same moment
claim: When discriminating differences between objects, the objects must be present simultaneously

quote: Both the discriminating power and the time of its exercise must be one and undivided
claim: The faculty that discriminates and its temporal exercise must be unified and undivided

quote: it may be objected, it is impossible that what is self-identical should be moved at one and the same time with contrary movements in so far as it is undivided
claim: Objection: Something self-identical cannot be moved by contrary movements simultaneously while remaining undivided

quote: if what is sweet be the quality perceived, it moves the sense or thought in this determinate way, while what is bitter moves it in a contrary way, and what is white in a different way
claim: Different perceptible qualities (sweet, bitter, white) move sense or thought in different or contrary ways

quote: Is it the case then that what discriminates, though both numerically one and indivisible, is at the same time divided in its being?
claim: The discriminating faculty may be numerically one and indivisible yet divided in its being

quote: In one sense, it is what is divided that perceives two separate objects at once, but in another sense it does so qua undivided
claim: The perceiving faculty perceives two objects simultaneously both qua divided and qua undivided

quote: for it is divisible in its being, but spatially and numerically undivided
claim: The discriminating faculty is divisible in being but spatially and numerically undivided

quote: But is not this impossible? For while it is true that what is self-identical and undivided may be both contraries at once potentially, it cannot be self-identical in its being
claim: Something self-identical may potentially contain contraries but cannot actually be self-identical while containing contraries in actuality

quote: it must lose its unity by being put into activity
claim: A thing loses its unity when it is actualized with contrary properties

quote: It is not possible to be at once white and black
claim: It is impossible for something to be white and black simultaneously

quote: therefore it must also be impossible for a thing to be affected at one and the same moment by the forms of both, assuming it to be the case that sensation and thinking are properly so described
claim: If sensation and thinking involve being affected by forms, it seems impossible to be affected by contrary forms simultaneously

quote: Just as what is called a point is, as being at once one and two, properly said to be divisible
claim: A point can be considered both one and two, and thus divisible (serving as an analogy)

quote: that which discriminates is qua undivided one, and active in a single moment of time, while qua divisible it twice over uses the same dot at one and the same time
claim: The discriminating faculty is undivided and active at one moment, but qua divisible uses the same point twice simultaneously

quote: So far then as it takes the limit as two, it discriminates two separate objects with what in a sense is separated; while so far as it takes it as one, it does so with what is one
claim: When the discriminating faculty treats the limit as two, it discriminates two objects with what is separated; when as one, with what is unified

quote: About the principle in virtue of which we say that animals are percipient, let this discussion suffice
claim: The preceding discussion adequately addresses the principle by which animals are said to perceive

quote: There are two distinctive peculiarities by reference to which we characterize the soul—(1) local movement and (2) thinking, understanding, and perceiving
claim: The soul is characterized by two distinctive features: local movement, and the complex of thinking/understanding/perceiving

quote: Thinking and understanding are regarded as akin to a form of perceiving
claim: Thinking and understanding are commonly considered to be similar to a kind of perceiving

quote: for in the one as well as the other the soul discriminates and is cognizant of something which is
claim: Both thinking and perceiving involve the soul discriminating and being cognizant of what exists

quote: Indeed the ancients go so far as to identify thinking and perceiving
claim: Ancient philosophers identified thinking with perceiving

quote: e.g. Empedocles says 'For 'tis in respect of what is present that man's wit is increased'
claim: Empedocles held that human intellect is increased in relation to what is present (to perception)

quote: and again 'Whence it befalls them from time to time to think diverse thoughts'
claim: Empedocles connected the diversity of thoughts to changing circumstances (of perception)

quote: and Homer's phrase 'For suchlike is man's mind' means the same
claim: Homer's phrase about the mind being 'suchlike' expresses the same view as Empedocles on thinking and perceiving

quote: They all look upon thinking as a bodily process like perceiving
claim: The ancients (Empedocles, Homer, and others) viewed thinking as a bodily process similar to perceiving

quote: and hold that like is understood as
claim: The ancients held a 'like knows like' principle whereby similar things understand similar things

quote: well as perceived by like, as I explained at the beginning of our discussion
claim: Predecessors held that perception occurs by like perceiving like

quote: Yet they ought at the same time to have accounted for error also
claim: Predecessors who explained perception by likeness failed to account for error

quote: for it is more intimately connected with animal existence and the soul continues longer in the state of error
claim: Error is more intimately connected with animal existence than truth, and the soul remains in error longer

quote: either whatever seems is true (and there are some who accept this)
claim: Some thinkers accept that whatever seems is true

quote: or error is contact with the unlike: for that is the opposite of the knowing of like by like
claim: If the like-by-like theory is correct, then error must be contact with the unlike

quote: But it seems that error as well as knowledge in respect to contraries is one and the same
claim: Error and knowledge regarding contraries belong to one and the same capacity

quote: That perceiving and understanding are not identical is therefore obvious
claim: Perceiving and understanding are not identical

quote: for the former is universal in the animal world, the latter is found in only a small division of it
claim: Perception is universal among animals while understanding is found only in a small subset

quote: Further, thinking is also distinct from perceiving—I mean that in which we find rightness and wrongness
claim: Thinking is distinct from perceiving, and thinking admits of rightness and wrongness

quote: rightness in understanding, knowledge, true opinion, wrongness in their opposites
claim: Rightness is found in understanding, knowledge, and true opinion; wrongness in their opposites

quote: for perception of the special objects of sense is always free from error, and is found in all animals
claim: Perception of the special/proper objects of sense is always free from error and is universal among animals

quote: while it is possible to think falsely as well as truly, and thought is found only where there is discourse of reason
claim: Thought can be either false or true and exists only in beings capable of rational discourse

quote: For imagination is different from either perceiving or discursive thinking
claim: Imagination is distinct from both perceiving and discursive thinking

quote: though it is not found without sensation, or judgement without it
claim: Imagination depends on sensation, and judgement depends on imagination

quote: That this activity is not the same kind of thinking as judgement is obvious
claim: Imagination is not the same kind of thinking as judgement

quote: For imagining lies within our own power whenever we wish (e.g. we can call up a picture, as in the practice of mnemonics by the use of mental images)
claim: Imagining is voluntary and within our power at will, as demonstrated by the use of mental images in mnemonics

quote: but in forming opinions we are not free: we cannot escape the alternative of falsehood or truth
claim: Opinion formation is not voluntary; we are constrained by truth and falsehood

quote: Further, when we think something to be fearful or threatening, emotion is immediately produced, and so too with what is encouraging
claim: Thinking something fearful or encouraging immediately produces corresponding emotion

quote: but when we merely imagine we remain as unaffected as persons who are looking at a painting of some dreadful or encouraging scene
claim: Mere imagination does not produce emotion, like viewing a painting of a dreadful scene leaves us unaffected

quote: Again within the field of judgement itself we find varieties—knowledge, opinion, under­standing, and their opposites
claim: Within judgement there are varieties: knowledge, opinion, understanding, and their opposites

quote: of the differences between these I must speak elsewhere
claim: The differences between varieties of judgement will be discussed elsewhere

quote: Thinking is different from perceiving and is held to be in part imagination, in part judgement
claim: Thinking differs from perceiving and is commonly held to consist partly of imagination and partly of judgement

quote: we must therefore first mark off the sphere of imagination and then speak of judgement
claim: The investigation must first define imagination before discussing judgement

quote: If then imagination is that in virtue of which an image arises for us, excluding metaphorical uses of the term
claim: Imagination is defined as that in virtue of which an image arises for us, setting aside metaphorical usage

quote: is it a single faculty or disposition relative to images, in virtue of which we discriminate and are either in error or not?
claim: A question is raised whether imagination is a single faculty or disposition through which we discriminate and may err

quote: The faculties in virtue of which we do this are sense, opinion, knowledge, thought
claim: The faculties by which we discriminate and may be in error are sense, opinion, knowledge, and thought

quote: That imagination is not sense is clear from the following considerations
claim: Imagination is not the same as sense

quote: Sense is either a faculty or an activity, e.g. sight or seeing: imagination takes place in the absence of both, as e.g. in dreams
claim: Sense is either faculty or activity (sight/seeing), but imagination occurs in the absence of both, as in dreams

quote: Again, sense is always present, imagination not
claim: Sense is always present in animals while imagination is not

quote: If actual imagination and actual sensation were the same, imagination would be found in all the brutes
claim: If imagination and sensation were identical, imagination would be found in all animals

quote: this is held not to be the case; e.g. it is not found in ants or bees or grubs
claim: Imagination is held not to be found in all animals, for example not in ants, bees, or grubs

quote: Again, sensations are always true, imaginations are for the most part false
claim: Sensations are always true while imaginations are for the most part false

quote: Once more, we do not, when sense functions precisely with regard to its object, say that we imagine it to be a man
claim: When sense functions precisely regarding its object, we do not say we imagine it to be something

quote: but rather when there is some failure ofaccuracy in its exercise—then it is either true or false
claim: We speak of imagining when there is some failure of accuracy in sense perception, and then it is either true or false

quote: visions appear to us even when our eyes are shut
claim: Visions or imaginings can occur even when our eyes are closed

quote: Neither is imagination any of the things that are never in error: e.g. knowledge or intelligence
claim: Imagination is not identical with knowledge or intelligence

quote: for imagination may be false
claim: Imagination can be false, unlike knowledge and intelligence which are never in error

quote: It remains therefore to see if it is opinion, for opinion may be either true or false
claim: Opinion is a candidate for what imagination is because both can be true or false

quote: opinion involves belief (for without belief in what we opine we cannot have an opinion)
claim: Opinion necessarily involves belief; one cannot have an opinion without believing it

quote: in the brutes though we often find imagination we never find belief
claim: Non-human animals have imagination but lack belief

quote: every opinion is accompanied by belief, belief by conviction, and conviction by discourse of reason
claim: Opinion requires belief, belief requires conviction, and conviction requires rational discourse

quote: there are some of the brutes in which we find imagination, without discourse of reason
claim: Some non-human animals possess imagination but lack the capacity for rational discourse

quote: imagination cannot, again, be opinion plus sensation, or opinion mediated by sensation, or a blend of opinion and sensation
claim: Imagination is not opinion combined with sensation, nor opinion mediated by sensation, nor a blend of both

quote: the content of the supposed opinion cannot be different from that of the sensation
claim: If imagination were a blend of opinion and sensation, the content of opinion would have to match the content of sensation

quote: imagination must be the blending of the perception of white with the opinion that it is white: it could scarcely be a blend of the opinion that it is good with the perception that it is white
claim: On the blending view, imagining white would require blending perception of white with opinion that it is white, not with unrelated opinions

quote: to imagine is therefore (on this view) identical with the thinking of exactly the same as what one perceives non-incidentally
claim: The blending view entails that imagining would be identical to thinking exactly what one perceives non-incidentally

quote: what we imagine is sometimes false though our contemporaneous judgement about it is true
claim: Imagination can be false even when our simultaneous judgment about the same thing is true

quote: we imagine the sun to be a foot in diameter though we are convinced that it is larger than the inhabited part of the earth
claim: We imagine the sun as a foot wide while simultaneously knowing it is larger than the inhabited earth

quote: either while the fact has not changed and the observer has neither forgotten nor lost belief in the true opinion which he had, that opinion has disappeared
claim: If imagination were opinion, one would have to say either the true opinion disappeared without forgetting or change in facts

quote: or if he retains it then his opinion is at once true and false
claim: If imagination were opinion, one would have to hold contradictory opinions (both true and false) simultaneously

quote: A true opinion, however, becomes false only when the fact alters without being noticed
claim: True opinion becomes false only when the underlying fact changes unnoticed

quote: Imagination is therefore neither any one of the states enumerated, nor compounded out of them
claim: Imagination is not identical with or compounded from sensation, knowledge, intelligence, or opinion

quote: since when one thing has been set in motion another thing may be moved by it
claim: Motion can be transmitted from one thing to another

quote: imagination is held to be a movement and to be impossible without sensation
claim: Imagination is a kind of movement that requires sensation

quote: to occur in beings that are percipient and to have for its content what can be perceived
claim: Imagination occurs only in perceiving beings and has perceivable content

quote: movement may be produced by actual sensation and that movement is necessarily similar in character to the sensation itself
claim: The movement of imagination is produced by actual sensation and resembles that sensation in character

quote: this movement cannot exist apart from sensation or in creatures that do not perceive
claim: The movement of imagination cannot exist independently of sensation or in non-perceiving creatures

quote: its possessor does and undergoes many things in virtue of it, and it is true and false
claim: The possessor of imagination acts and is affected by it, and imagination can be true or false

quote: Perception of the special objects of sense is never in error or admits the least possible amount of falsehood
claim: Perception of proper sensibles (special objects of each sense) is never or almost never in error

quote: perception that what is incidental to the objects of perception is incidental to them: in this case certainly we may be deceived
claim: Perception of incidental properties of sensible objects is susceptible to error

quote: the perception that there is white before us cannot be false, the perception that what is white is this or that may be false
claim: Perceiving whiteness as such cannot be false, but perceiving what the white thing is can be false

quote: the perception of the common attributes which accompany the incidental objects to which the special sensibles attach (I mean e.g. of movement and magnitude)
claim: There is a third type of perception: perception of common sensibles like movement and magnitude

quote: it is in respect of these that the greatest amount of sense-illusion is possible
claim: The greatest possibility of perceptual error occurs with respect to common sensibles

quote: The motion which is due to the activity of sense in these three modes of its exercise will differ
claim: Motion derived from sense activity differs according to three modes of exercise

quote: the first kind of derived motion is free from error while the sensation is present
claim: The first kind of motion derived from sense is free from error while sensation is present

quote: the others may be erroneous whether it is present or absent, especially when the object of perception is far off
claim: Other kinds of derived motion may be erroneous whether sensation is present or absent, especially when the perceived object is distant

quote: imagination must be a movement resulting from an actual exercise of a power of sense
claim: Imagination is a movement resulting from an actual exercise of a power of sense

quote: As sight is the most highly developed sense
claim: Sight is the most highly developed sense

quote: the name (jxxvTctola (imagination) has been formed from (f>aos (light) because it is not possible to see without light
claim: The word 'phantasia' (imagination) derives etymologically from 'phaos' (light) because seeing requires light

quote: imaginations remain in the organs of sense and resemble sensations
claim: Imaginations persist in the sense organs and resemble sensations

quote: animals in their actions are largely guided by them
claim: Animals are largely guided by imaginations in their actions

quote: some (i.e. the brutes) because of the non-existence in them of thought
claim: Brute animals are guided by imagination because thought does not exist in them

quote: others (i.e. men) because of the temporary eclipse in them of thought by feeling or disease or sleep
claim: Humans are sometimes guided by imagination when thought is temporarily eclipsed by feeling, disease, or sleep

quote: Turning now to the part of the soul with which the soul knows and (whether this is separable from the others in definition only, or spatially as well)
claim: It is a question whether the knowing part of the soul is separable from other parts in definition only or also spatially

quote: we have to inquire what differentiates this part, and how thinking can take place
claim: Inquiry is needed into what differentiates the thinking part of the soul and how thinking occurs

quote: If thinking is like perceiving, it must be either a process in which the soul is acted upon by what is capable of being thought, or a process different from but analogous to that
claim: If thinking resembles perceiving, it must be either a passive process where soul is acted upon by the thinkable, or an analogous but different process

quote: The thinking part of the soul must therefore be, while impassible, capable of receiving the form of an object
claim: The thinking part of the soul must be impassible yet capable of receiving the form of an object

quote: must be potentially identical in character with its object without being the object
claim: The thinking part must be potentially identical in character with its object without being the object itself

quote: Thought must be related to what is thinkable, as sense is to what is sensible
claim: The relation between thought and the thinkable is analogous to the relation between sense and the sensible

quote: since everything is a possible object of thought
claim: Everything is a possible object of thought

quote: mind in order, as Anaxagoras says, to dominate, that is, to know, must be pure from all admixture
claim: Anaxagoras held that the mind must be pure from all admixture in order to dominate and know

quote: for the co-presence of what is alien to its nature is a hindrance and a block
claim: The co-presence of what is alien to the mind's nature hinders and blocks it

quote: it follows that it can have no nature of its own, other than that of having a certain capacity
claim: The mind has no nature of its own other than having a certain capacity

quote: that in the soul which is called thought (by thought I mean that whereby the soul thinks and judges) is, before it thinks, not actually any real thing
claim: Thought (that by which the soul thinks and judges) is not actually any real thing before it thinks

quote: For this reason it cannot reasonably be regarded as blended with the body
claim: The thinking part of the soul cannot reasonably be regarded as blended with the body

quote: if so, it would acquire some quality, e.g, warmth or cold, or even have an organ like the sensitive faculty: as it is, it has none
claim: If thought were blended with body, it would acquire qualities like warmth or cold, or have a bodily organ like the sensitive faculty—but it has none

quote: It was a good idea to call the soul 'the place of forms'
claim: It was a good idea to call the soul 'the place of forms'

quote: though this description holds only of the thinking soul, and even this is the forms only potentially, not actually
claim: The description 'place of forms' applies only to the thinking soul, and even then only potentially, not actually

quote: Observation of the sense-organs and their employment reveals a distinction between the impassibility of the sensitive faculty and that of the faculty of thought
claim: Observation of sense organs reveals a distinction between the impassibility of the sensitive faculty and that of the faculty of thought

quote: After strong stimulation of a sense we are less able to exercise it than before
claim: After strong stimulation of a sense we are less able to exercise that sense than before

quote: in the case of a loud sound we cannot hear easily immediately after, or in the case of a bright colour or a powerful odour we cannot see or smell
claim: After a loud sound we cannot hear easily, and after bright colors or powerful odors we cannot see or smell well

quote: in the case of thought thinking about an object that is highly thinkable renders it more and not less able afterwards to think of objects that are less thinkable
claim: Thinking about highly thinkable objects makes one more (not less) able to think about less thinkable objects

quote: the reason is that while the faculty of sensation is dependent upon the body, thought is separable from it
claim: The faculty of sensation is dependent upon the body, while thought is separable from it
